title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation fraud in which AI-generated deepfake images and videos were used to fabricate a news article and interview featuring two real, named public figures. The fake article attributed statements to Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock and ABC presenter Alan Kohler promoting an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform called Boulder Sparhaven. Neither the interview nor the article existed. The failure mode is the use of AI tools to manufacture convincing surface-level authenticity, including realistic likenesses and plausible editorial formats, in order to deceive consumers into trusting a fraudulent investment product.

The fraud operated entirely outside any regulated deployment context. There was no licensed platform, no human editorial check, and no institutional oversight of the content before it reached potential victims. Detection depended entirely on the targets independently verifying the existence of the interview or checking whether Boulder Sparhaven held a financial license. ASIC's removal of nearly 19,400 scams in a single year, a figure 182 percent higher than the year before, indicates that the volume of such fabrications is outpacing reactive takedown efforts.

What is not established is who created or operated the Boulder Sparhaven platform, how many people were harmed, or whether any individuals have been identified or charged in connection with this specific incident.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article claimed Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock had a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The article and interview never actually occurred. This type of scam is becoming increasingly common and sophisticated, according to the Australian Securities and Investments Commission. Scammers use artificial intelligence to create deepfake images and videos of well-known Australians to promote fraudulent investments.

ASIC removed 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase from the previous year, with phishing scams jumping 279 percent and fake investment platforms rising 151 percent. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, businesswoman Gina Rinehart, and finance presenter Alan Kohler are among the most commonly impersonated public figures. Scammers build elaborate fake websites, news articles, and reviews to deceive consumers into providing personal information and money. ASIC advises people to verify financial licenses through official registers before investing and not to trust investment opportunities based solely on celebrity endorsements.
